div.p: Due to the critical nature of real-time systems, there is an ever growing burden on the designer to not only guarantee that the tasks would meet their deadlines at design time, but would continue to do so as the system evolves. This implies that the schedulability analysis has to be robust. In this study we identify the sensitivity of schedulability analysis to the task execution times. The impact, this parameter has on the schedulability analysis is captured by formulating a general scaling problem. This problem is shown to relate to the problems of scalability, portability and execution time estimation. A technique to solve this general problem is developed. A proof of correctness and optimality of the technique is presented.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: A task-set in a real-time system is said to be schedulable if the deadlines of all its tasks can be met. Given the estimates of task requirements (e.g., execution time, resource requirements, deadline, and periodicity), schedulability analysis attempts to determine whether the given task set is schedulable. While schedulability analysis is an essential tool in real-time system design, its stringent requirements on the accuracy of the task specification often pose problems during its usage.

While some task parameters such as the arrival time, periodicity, and deadline are largely intrinsic to a task, parameters such as the execution time of a task are a function of the task (the algorithm used, the programming language the task is coded in, the particular compiler used etc.), as well as the system architecture (MIPS, Memory size, cache effectiveness etc.). Hence, it may be easier to estimate the intrinsic parameters more accurately than the software and hardware dependent ones.

In order to deal with the iinpredictability (or inaccuracies) of task execution times, researchers (and practioners) often assume worst-case execution times for schedulability analysis. While the worst-case execution path does give a bound on the execution time, *This work is sponsored by a grant from NASA (NAG-1-1114) in general it is not the one most frequently taken [lo]. The point to note, therefore, is that any guarantees that schedulability analysis makes about a task set are sensitive to and closely coupled with assumptions about the processor architecture and the estimations about the requirements of the task set. Also, as realtime systems evolve, the functionality of tasks change and there is a nagging question of how this would reflect on the schedulability of a task.

While it is possible to make repeated schedulability runs with different sets of parameters, this is computationally expensive. In this paper, we propose a solution technique that can be used to extend the validity of a prior schedulability analysis when (i new cution times have increased (scalability), or (111 only commodating task execution time variances).

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 gives the problems solved and the general scaling problem that captures them. In section 3 we suggest a technique to solve the general problem and also demonstrate its effectiveness (correctness and optimality). In section 4 we show how the general problem helps us address the issues of scalability, portability and task execution time estimation. Section 5 summarizes this work and suggests future extensions.

div.head: Problem Statement
div.p: Before we state the problem, we would like to draw the readers interest to three important problems whose relevance will be made clear in the later part of the paper. The three important problems are:

div.head: Scalability
div.p: Often schedulability analysis in real-time systems is done off-line and the individual task execution times are assumed to be constant. However, we are often faced with the situation where, as the system is evolving, the data handled by a task changes. Such changes could result in increased computation and communication requirements of tasks. It is tedious and impractical to perform the schedulability analysis every time there is a change. Therefore, one of the most often asked questions during the maintenance of real-time systems are:
(i) By how much can a task execution time be increased maintaining its schedulability?

Using the worst-case execution times of tasks for schedulability analysis is a rather pessimistic approach. In most applications, the worst case path (through the code) is not the most frequently traversed path. In order to handle this problem, we can make use of the statistical estimation techniques for finding the execution time. There should be some way of accommodating the information about the variance in the schedulability analysis. Therefore, the question that needs to be answered is: 3 Suggested Technique

Further, they propose an iterative mechanism which can be avoided. We have devised a technique, which not only finds a correct result but also finds the optimal scaling factor for most cases. We also give a formal proof for its correctness and effectiveness.

div.head: Applications
div.p: The applicability of this solution technique in solving the problems of scalability, estimation and portability in real-time systems is discussed here. The relationship between this problem and the problem of scalability of task execution time is straightforward. As a system evolves, more and more functionality is added resulting in either increasing the number of tasks or adding enhancements to the already existing tasks, or both. The first choice would imply that the schedulability analysis has to be performed again, however the second choice would reflect itself as a scaling of the execution time of the task in question.

The second problem we wish to address, relates to the estimation of task execution times. The difficulty in finding the execution times of programs in general and real-time programs in particular [SI has been emphasized by many researchers in the past. It has become imperative that any such estimations have to be qualified by taking into consideration the variance. This new parameter can impact the schedula-Finally the issue of portability of real-time applications is dealt with. Due to the life critical conditions under which real-time systems operate, it is often difficult or in most cases impossible to test the final system in operation. A reasonable alternative to testing the system is to build a prototype of the system. In or- der to facilitate a thorough (possibly exhaustive) testing we could build the prototype to be a scaled up faster) realization of the target system. We can now 6 o a schedulability analysis of the prototype system and seek to extend the results to the target system. Clearly, the schedulability analysis holds if the target system is faster than the prototype. If however the target system is slower (which is often the case), then we observe that such a change in processor speed (and other architectural parameters) would reflect as an increase in execution time. For instance, the execution time for a task running on the prototype (a faster processor say) could be 0.6 times that on the target system. Thus, the problem reduces to the general scalability problem.

Following are a couple of practical scenarios where our technique can be used. Imagine an air traffic control system. With each additional flight that has to be monitored, the amount of radar information to be processed also increases. Even if the schedulability analysis is performed assuming the maximum possible flights (at the time of analysis), any change to this number (due to one of the many reasons identified here) as the system evolves means that the analysis has to be performed again. However, so long as a change in radar information causes the processing increase to be within bounds, the schedulability analysis holds. As a second example consider a distributed real-time system where we have a distributed load balancing mechanism that uses state-change broadcasts [ll]. If the size of the state-change message to be broadcasted has to be increased, one has to study the effect this change has on the schedulability of the message (whether the message meets its deadline).

The technique we have developed can be easily extended to incorporate the concept of blockang delays [3]. Blocking delay refers to the amount of time a high priority task has to wait while a lower priority task uses the processor (or some other resource). This phenomena is a consequence of synchronization in real-time systems and is popularly referred to as priority inversion. For a detailed study of the issues of synchronization in real-time systems, please refer to RajKumar et. al. [lo] K. Ramamritham, J. A. Stankovic, and W. Zhao.
